title: The puzzle of trait covariation: a commentary on ‘Elevated CO2, warming and drought differentially impact reproductive and vegetative economic traits in two grassland species’
content: A central aim of functional plant ecology is to identify the main axes of trait variation that define ecological strategies. Influential frameworks such as the leaf economics spectrum and competitor–stress tolerator–ruderal (CSR) strategy theory have been built largely on vegetative traits, while other dimensions of plant form and function, most notably floral traits, have received comparatively less attention (E-Vojtkó et al., 2022). Yet, flowers are a fundamental component of plant fitness and mediate interactions with pollinators and other biotic agents. Since Berg’s hypothesis that vegetative and floral traits respond largely to distinct selective pressures (Berg, 1960), subsequent studies have reported either decoupling (Roddy et al., 2013) or covariation between vegetative and floral traits associated with size constraints and pollination strategies (Fantinato et al., 2025). More recently, the integration of floral traits into broader trait-based frameworks has started to gain momentum (e.g. Liu et al., 2025), reflecting a growing recognition of the need for a whole-plant perspective.
